translations.answer: The video shows continuous pose transition and center of mass (CoM) movement, but the commentary suggests the action may have been choreographed and rehearsed; no external disturbances, failure counts, state/contact curves, or controller information were provided, so only qualitative observations can be formed, and robust recovery cannot be proven.
translations.applicability: Applicable to the strength of evidence for human-like demonstration video reviews.
translations.credibility.rationale: The explanation has not closed or there is a conflict; only problem clues are formed.
translations.details.attempts.0: A qualitative observation was made using a dance video.
translations.details.diagnostics.0: Focus on hip recovery and transitions between poses.
translations.details.environments.0: Live dance demonstration; continuous arm/leg movements.
translations.details.limits.0: Cannot infer algorithm robustness or communication real-time from the video.
translations.details.outcomes.0: The demonstration maintains balance, but it may have been choreographed and rehearsed.
translations.details.problem_statements.0: A single static gait metric cannot evaluate multi-poses continuous switching.
translations.details.safety_notes.0: The demonstration does not equal anti-disturbance validation; independent push, recovery, and failure testing is required.
translations.details.suspected_causes.0: Continuous center of mass (CoM) transfer imposes stronger transient requirements on balance control.
translations.details.symptoms.0: The original post did not report failures, only observed no visible reset.
translations.media_summaries.0: The screenshot is a text analysis of pose transitions, hip recovery, and continuous balance, without showing state curves or disturbance experiments.
translations.source.title: Why can't we judge human-like WBC robustness just from a dance video without errors?
